title.full: ASEAN Green Future Project Phase 2.2 Report, Optimising Malaysia's Electrifying Future

publisher.full: Sustainable Development Solutions Network and ClimateWorks Centre

description: Exploratory MY power pathway simulating NETR/MyRER targets as inputs; no emissions constraint.
pathwayDescription:
Exploratory Malaysian pathway (2019–2050) that feeds NETR/MyRER targets into a LEAP simulation with no emissions cap: RE shares of 31%/40%/70% for 2025/2035/2050, no new coal or diesel, coal out by 2050, efficiency standards and 80% xEV fleet share. Demand rises 152% to 393 TWh. A fixed merit order produces a 72 GW solar build, yet power emissions grow from 85 to 108 MtCO2e and investment tops USD 250bn, over USD 100bn in fossil.

The ASEAN Green Future regional research project is run by the United Nations Sustainable Development Solutions Network, Climateworks Centre, and local researchers from leading universities. The project develops national policy analysis and near-zero pathways that are meant to provide policy recommendations and support policy makers.

coreDrivers.policies: Target shares: NETR/MyRER capacity mix and RE targets (31% in 2025, 40% in 2035, 70% in 2050), incl. MyRER’s 2.5x higher bioenergy targets, are exogenous inputs. Phase-out: no new coal or diesel; coal out by 2050, diesel by 2045 via natural retirement. Efficiency: NETR’s 23% energy-intensity gain for industry and commercial (EECA) and NEEAP household appliance targets. Transport: 80% xEV share of 4- and 2-wheelers, 60% public-transport share, 5% hydrogen heavy vehicles, B30 biodiesel.
coreDrivers.investmentChange: Cumulative power generation investment exceeds USD 250 bn, with more than USD 100 bn in fossil fuel.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: GDP, population, urbanisation (76% in 2018 to 90% by 2060) and sectoral value added drive electricity demand to 393 TWh in 2050 (+152% vs 2019), with services and industry making up 79% of the increase. Services are capped at 65% of GDP and agriculture floored at 5% from 2031, leaving industry at 30% (calibrated on Australia and Singapore). Sources: government projections, UN World Urbanization Prospects, World Bank data, LEAP defaults; assumptions are shared by all three pathways.
coreDrivers.otherDrivers: Simulation-mode dispatch and reserve rules: the modeller fixes the merit order (1: solar+BESS and wind; 2: coal, gas, hydro, geothermal, MSW, biomass, biogas; 3: diesel), and LEAP adds any capacity needed to hold the planning reserve margin in the modeller's addition order. This configuration produces EP's larger fleet (137.8 GW vs 125.2 GW in OEP) and a 72 GW solar build that exceeds NETR's 56 GW. It is a model-configuration assumption, not a policy, cost or macroeconomic driver.

dependencies.dependency_description: EP is built on the NETR, MyRER, NBAP, HETR and EECA policy set, which supplies its renewable capacity targets, coal moratorium and efficiency targets and so enables grid decarbonisation up to a 66% RE capacity share in 2050. The report judges this set insufficient for near-zero power: EP still emits 108 MtCO2e from generation in 2050 with gas at 55% of output, and NETR's positioning of gas as a bridge fuel needs re-evaluation.

The report records regulatory weaknesses that limit EP's demand-side efficiency: weak enforcement of building rules, limited financing for energy performance contracts and an EECA covering only 21% of commercial consumption and under 1% of users. On supply, biogas grid connection is unattractive because the FiT (RM0.28–0.32/kWh) sits below base tariffs. These are described rather than modelled as constraints on EP's power mix.

EP relies on gas for 55% of 2050 generation, exposing it to gas prices and Malaysia's growing import dependence (about 25% of gas needs in 2023); the report flags stranded-asset risk for new gas plants. EP has the highest cost of the two existing-policy cases: USD 257bn real cumulative investment and 8.8 US cents/kWh in 2050, against regulated tariffs of 4.2–12.0 US cents/kWh and RM2bn of consumer subsidies in H1 2024.

The report notes that hydropower can disrupt ecosystems and displace indigenous communities and needs long planning. EP expands hydro to 15.1 GW in 2050, above NETR's 11 GW, so the concern applies, but the report does not treat acceptance as constraining EP.

EP imposes demand-side adoption exogenously — 80% xEV share, 60% public-transport modal share, efficient lighting at 55% by 2025 and electric cooking reaching 60% (urban) and 40% (rural) by 2060 — which raises transport electricity from 1 to 33 TWh. These raise power demand but do not constrain power decarbonisation in EP.

Integrating EP's 72 GW of solar needs grid modernisation, storage and interconnection, yet EP holds only 0.50 GW of batteries. The report identifies Sabah's single 275 kV backbone as a bottleneck, lists existing interconnections (MY–TH 380 MW, MY–SG 1,000 MW, Sarawak–West Kalimantan 80–110 MW) and cites EV-charging needs (10,000 public chargers by 2025). No hourly dispatch or curtailment output is reported.

Battery storage is the only not-yet-scaled technology in EP (0.50 GW in 2050), supported by pilots such as TNB's 400 MWh and Sarawak's 60 MW systems; the report notes batteries currently suit seconds-to-hours storage only, limiting their role in this gas-backed system.

EP depends on natural gas for 55% of 2050 generation while Malaysia already imports about a quarter of its gas, so supply security is a real dependency. Domestic renewable resources are ample for EP's build: solar potential 269 GW, hydro 16.1 GW (EP uses 15.1 GW), and EP's 1.8 GW biomass is within SEDA's 2.3 GW estimate.

Hydropower supplies about 20% of EP's 2050 generation and is exposed to drought and rainfall variability; the report cites the recent global fall in hydro output from droughts and recommends diversification, water management and demand-side management. Climate impacts and resilience were not modelled.
